units.title: Unit 09 — The body and movement
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 9. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Identify major body parts in labelled diagrams and everyday descriptions.
Describe movements of the head and face, including breathing, smiling, laughing, crying and yawning.
Distinguish nodding from shaking the head and associate them with common communicative meanings.
Use natural expressions such as shake hands, blow your nose, comb your hair, fold your arms and wave to somebody.
Recognise silent letters and irregular past forms in relevant body and movement vocabulary.

items.example: The human body needs regular exercise.
items.note: The whole physical structure of a person.

items.example: Wear sunscreen to protect your skin.
items.note: The outer covering of the body; usually uncountable in this meaning.

items.example: A drop of sweat ran down his forehead.
items.note: The part of the face above the eyes.

items.example: The baby had rosy cheeks.
items.note: One of the two soft sides of the face.

items.example: He rested his chin on his hand.
items.note: The lowest part of the face, below the mouth.

items.example: Her lips were dry in the cold weather.
items.note: Plural of lip; the two soft edges of the mouth.

items.example: She carried her bag over one shoulder.
items.note: The part where the arm joins the body.

items.example: My neck feels stiff after sitting all day.
items.note: The part joining the head to the body.

items.example: He felt a sharp pain in his chest.
items.note: The front upper part of the body, containing the heart and lungs.

items.example: She noticed a mark on her left breast.
items.note: A part of the chest, particularly developed in adult women; also used in medical descriptions.

items.example: He leaned on the desk with one elbow.
items.note: The joint in the middle of the arm.

items.example: This belt is too loose around my waist.
items.note: The narrower area between the ribs and hips.

items.example: The child landed on his bottom.
items.note: An everyday, relatively informal term for the part of the body you sit on.

items.example: She put one hand on her hip.
items.note: The area at each side of the body below the waist.

items.example: He wears a watch on his left wrist.
items.note: The joint connecting the hand to the arm; the initial w is silent.

items.example: She held the paper between her thumb and finger.
items.note: The short, thick finger at the side of the hand; the final b is silent.

items.example: He hurt his knee while playing football.
items.note: The joint in the middle of the leg; the initial k is silent.

items.example: She twisted her ankle on the stairs.
items.note: The joint between the leg and foot.

items.example: The back of his shoe rubbed against his heel.
items.note: The back part of the foot, below the ankle.

items.example: I hit my toe on the table leg.
items.note: One of the five digits on a foot.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: He turned his head towards the noise.
items.note: The top part of the body containing the brain, eyes and mouth.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: Open your mouth so the dentist can check your teeth.
items.note: The part of the face used for speaking, eating and breathing.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: My nose is blocked because I have a cold.
items.note: The part of the face used for smelling and breathing.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: Her face looked tired after the long journey.
items.note: The front part of the head.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: Try to breathe slowly and calmly.
items.note: A verb; distinguish breathe /briːð/ from the noun breath /breθ/.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: Breathe in deeply before you start.
items.note: To take air into your lungs; opposite of breathe out.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: Breathe out gently after three seconds.
items.note: To push air out of your lungs; opposite of breathe in.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: She smiled when she saw the surprise.
items.note: A facial expression showing pleasure or friendliness.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: The receptionist smiled at the visitors.
items.note: Use the preposition at when identifying the person who receives the smile.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: Everyone laughed when the dog stole the hat.
items.note: Usually expresses amusement; note the British pronunciation /lɑːf/.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: They laughed at the joke.
items.note: Can refer to finding something funny; laughing at a person may sound unkind.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: The little boy cried when his toy broke.
items.note: To produce tears because of sadness, pain or another strong feeling.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: She nodded to show she agreed.
items.note: To move your head up and down; past tense: nodded.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: If you agree, just nod your head.
items.note: Usually communicates agreement or yes in many cultures.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: He shook his head when they asked him to join.
items.note: Moving your head from side to side often communicates no or disagreement.

items.section: B · Mouth, face and head movements
items.example: I started to yawn during the late meeting.
items.note: To open the mouth widely and breathe in, often because of tiredness or boredom.

items.pt: apertar as mãos; cumprimentar com aperto de mão
items.example: The visitors shook hands after the meeting.
items.note: Usually describes a greeting or a sign of agreement. Past tense: shook hands.

items.example: I shook hands with the new manager.
items.note: The preposition with identifies the other person.

items.example: Please comb your hair before the photograph.
items.note: The b in comb is silent.

items.example: He used a tissue to blow his nose.
items.note: Common expression for clearing your nose; past tense: blew.

items.example: She folded her arms while she waited.
items.note: To put one arm across the other in front of your body.

items.example: We waved to our friends from the train.
items.note: Raise and move your hand to greet someone or say goodbye.

items.example: He raised his right hand to ask a question.
items.note: The part at the end of the arm, including the fingers and thumb.

items.example: She carried the shopping bags in both arms.
items.note: Plural of arm; the upper limbs of the body.

items.example: He has thick, dark hair.
items.note: Usually uncountable when referring to all the hair on someone's head.

items.example: Running made him breathe more quickly.
items.note: The activity used in exercise 9.4 to explain faster breathing.

units.title: Unit 10 — Describing appearance
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 10. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Choose appropriate adjectives for describing physical attractiveness and appearance.
Use tactful expressions when talking about appearance, weight and body size.
Describe height and weight using medium height, average, roughly, approximately, weigh and just under.
Distinguish hair colours and textures while treating hair as uncountable in ordinary descriptions.
Ask what someone looks like and describe shoulders, athletic appearance and smart clothing.
Understand the approximate meaning of the suffix -ish in tallish, longish and twentyish.

items.example: His appearance has changed since last summer.
items.note: How a person looks; not the same as personality or character.

items.example: She thought the singer was very attractive.
items.note: A neutral positive adjective for someone's looks.

items.example: He is a good-looking actor.
items.note: Common for men or women; normally written with a hyphen.

items.example: They chose a pretty dress for the party.
items.note: Often used of women, girls, or things; it may sound inappropriate for some adult men.

items.example: The bride looked beautiful in the photographs.
items.note: A strong positive description of beauty, especially used of women or things.

items.example: You look gorgeous in that colour.
items.note: A very strong, often enthusiastic word for attractiveness.

items.example: Her brother is a handsome young man.
items.note: Especially common when describing an attractive man.

items.example: He regretted calling another person ugly.
items.note: A direct, often hurtful description of appearance; use tact.

items.example: He described himself as an ordinary-looking person.
items.note: Less harsh than ugly, but does not mean especially attractive.

items.example: The word fat can offend people when used about their bodies.
items.note: A direct description of body size; frequently impolite when referring to people.

items.example: The doctor said he was slightly overweight.
items.note: Usually more tactful than fat; can also be a clinical description.

items.example: They make a very good-looking couple.
items.note: A natural collocation describing the appearance of two people together.

items.example: You look gorgeous tonight.
items.note: Look + adjective describes how someone appears at a particular moment.

items.example: The doorway is only two metres in height.
items.note: A noun; compare the adjective high or tall.

items.example: The parcel's weight is written on the label.
items.note: Noun; the related verb is weigh, pronounced /weɪ/.

items.example: The suitcase weighs nearly twenty kilos.
items.note: The letters gh are silent; say weigh seventy kilos, not weigh with seventy kilos.

items.example: My cousin is taller than me.
items.note: Used for someone's height; comparative: taller.

items.example: His sister is quite short.
items.note: For height; short also has other meanings such as brief.

items.example: There were roughly thirty people at the event.
items.note: Can mean approximately when giving an estimate.

items.example: The village is approximately ten kilometres away.
items.note: A more formal alternative to about or roughly.

items.example: She is just under sixty kilograms.
items.note: Used for a quantity slightly lower than the number that follows.

items.example: The journey takes just over an hour.
items.note: A useful contrast with just under; included as an explicit teaching extension.

items.example: The witness described the man as medium height.
items.note: Neither especially tall nor especially short; say of medium height or medium height.

items.example: His height is about average for his age.
items.note: Used for what is normal or typical compared with others.

items.example: My height is about average.
items.note: A natural answer when someone asks about typical size or height.

items.example: She asked, 'How tall are you?'
items.note: Use how tall, not how high, when asking about a person's height.

items.example: He is one metre eighty tall.
items.note: Informal spoken way to express 1.80 metres in British English.

items.example: She has very thick hair.
items.note: Usually uncountable when referring to the hair on a person's head: not hairs in this sense.

items.example: She has blonde hair.
items.note: Blonde is common for hair colour; blond is also an accepted spelling.

items.example: He has short blond hair.
items.note: An alternative spelling; blond has traditionally been common for males.

items.example: He had fair hair when he was a child.
items.note: For hair, fair means light in colour; it has other meanings in different contexts.

items.example: My aunt has brown hair.
items.note: Brown describes a hair colour between blonde and black.

items.example: She has dark hair and green eyes.
items.note: Dark can describe brown or black hair.

items.example: Her son has straight black hair.
items.note: Say black hair, without a before hair.

items.example: His straight hair reaches his shoulders.
items.note: Straight hair is not curly or wavy.

items.example: She has long wavy hair.
items.note: Hair with loose waves; usually less tightly curled than curly hair.

items.example: He has thick curly hair.
items.note: Hair that grows in curls or ringlets.

items.example: He has long hair tied back in a ponytail.
items.note: Do not use an article before hair when describing all the hair on a person's head.

items.example: My sister prefers short hair in summer.
items.note: A common way to describe hair length.

items.example: What does he look like? Is he tall or short?
items.note: Asks for a physical description, not what someone enjoys or is like as a person.

items.pt: parecer com; ter a aparência de
items.example: He looks like his older brother.
items.note: Use look like + noun/pronoun, or look + adjective for appearance.

items.example: The new colleague is tallish, with brown hair.
items.note: The suffix -ish softens tall to mean fairly or rather tall.

items.example: He has a broad back.
items.note: Opposite in this context: narrow.

items.example: The door is too narrow for the large table.
items.note: Opposite of broad or wide; also used about body features.

items.example: She is athletic and has broad shoulders.
items.note: A common expression for shoulders that are wide across.

items.example: The jacket was loose on his narrow shoulders.
items.note: Useful contrast with broad shoulders.

items.example: She looks athletic because she swims regularly.
items.note: Describes someone looking strong and fit, often from sport.

items.example: He looked smart in his new jacket.
items.note: For appearance, smart means neat and stylish; not necessarily intelligent.

items.example: They always dress well for formal events.
items.note: Dress as a verb refers to the clothes someone chooses to wear.

items.example: He is quite tall for his age.
items.note: Degree adverb; its force can vary with context and intonation.

items.example: The room was rather cold.
items.note: Often marks a moderate or somewhat unexpected degree.

items.example: His hair was longish but easy to manage.
items.note: The ending -ish means approximately or somewhat, depending on the base.

items.example: The man at the reception desk looked twentyish.
items.note: Informal approximate age formed with -ish.

items.example: You look smart in that coat.
items.note: Look + adjective describes someone's appearance at the moment.

items.example: She looked strong and healthy after months of training.
items.note: A descriptive phrase closely connected to the meaning of athletic.

items.example: He wore a dark suit to the interview.
items.note: In exercise 10.1, a smart suit is part of describing someone as smart.
